p.seg: A body of one *rèn* in height
is enough to see its governance.
Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* is cautious about his few (thoughts and actions).
The Dao in relation to people,
is quite simple and easy.
Cultivating it
is not like mining gold and carving jade, involving difficult journeys;
it is not like seeking profit and wealth, competing with noisy煩ness.
It meets without seeking,
it flourishes without summoning,
the four seasons silently bring it to completion,
it is trustworthy without words,
its virtue matches Heaven and Earth,
its merit equals the four seasons,
its name joins the sun and moon.
This is why Yú Shùn and Dà Yǔ rose from commoners to the imperial throne,
shedding plain cloth and donning embroidered garments.
Therefore, an ancient saying goes:
"The nobility of supreme virtue—
where can it not succeed?
The glory of supreme virtue—
where can it not be accomplished?"
Later *jūnzǐ*,
even if they do not attain it in practice,
will still aspire to it, so they say.
The zither and lute sound,
and do not lose their tune because there is no one listening;
benevolence and righteousness are practiced,
and do not vanish because there are no people present.
Therefore, when the strings break, the musical notes of *gōng* and *shāng* disappear;
when the body dies, benevolence and righteousness are abandoned.
Zēngzǐ said:
"The *shì*'s burden is heavy and the road is long.
《Zhì Xué Dì Yī》
In the past, noble men achieved virtue and established conduct,
and though their bodies perished, their names did not fade.
What was the reason for this?
Learning.
Learning is the means by which to clarify the spirit, articulate thoughts, cultivate emotions, and understand reason.
It is the foremost duty of the sages.
When the people are first born,
they are ignorant and unknowing.
It is like a treasure hidden in a dark room,
where one seeks something but cannot find it.
When the white sun shines,
then all things are clearly distinguished.
Learning is the white sun of the mind,
therefore the former kings established education officials,
in charge of teaching the sons of the state,
teaching them the six virtues,
namely wisdom, benevolence, sagacity, righteousness, centrality, and harmony;
teaching them the six actions,
namely filial piety, brotherly love, concord, affinal affinity, trust, and compassion;
teaching them the six arts,
namely ritual, music, archery, horsemanship, writing, and mathematics;
when these three teachings are complete, the way of humanity is fulfilled.
Learning is like ornamentation,
if a vessel is not ornamented, it cannot be considered beautiful to look at,
if a person does not learn, they cannot have fine virtue.
Having fine virtue,
therefore one can manage human relationships;
being beautiful to look at,
therefore one can serve the spirits.
Therefore, the Book [of Documents] says:
"If one is making coffin wood,
after diligent cutting and shaping,
then one applies red and ochre paint."
Indeed, after hearing the sound of the *huáng zhōng* bell,
one then knows the subtlety of striking an earthenware pot;
after seeing the patterns of the dragon robe,
one then knows the coarseness of wearing sackcloth;
after experiencing the teaching of the school,
Ránhòu zhī bù xué zhī kùn; Then you will realize the trouble of not learning;
gù xuézhě rú dēngshān yān, therefore, learning is like climbing a mountain,
dòng ér yì gāo; moving and becoming higher;
rú wùmèi yān, like waking from sleep,
jiǔ ér yù zú. the longer it goes, the more fulfilled you become.
Gù suǒ yóu lái, Looking back at the path you came from,
zé yǎorán qí yuǎn, it seems vaguely far away;
yǐ qí nán ér xiè zhī, if you slacken because it is difficult,
wù qiě fēi yǐ! you will be mistaken and wrong!
Shī yún: The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Gāoshān yǎng zhǐ, "High mountains are looked up to,
jǐngxíng háng zhǐ." Great roads are followed."
Hào xué zhī wèi yě. This speaks of the love of learning.
Yǐlì ér sī yuǎn, Leaning and standing while thinking of distant places,
bùrú sù xíng zhī bì zhì yě; is not as good as quickly traveling there, which will surely get you there;
jiǎo shǒu ér xùn fēi, Tilting your head and following flight,
bùrú xiū yì zhī bì huò yě; is not as good as cultivating your wings, which will surely allow you to fly;
gū jū ér yuàn zhì, Living alone and wishing for wisdom,
bùrú wù xué zhī bì dá yě; is not as good as diligently learning, which will surely achieve it;
gù jūnzǐ xīn bù gǒu yuàn, therefore, a virtuous person does not make frivolous wishes in his heart,
bì yǐ qiúxué; but is certain to seek learning;
shēn bù gǒu dòng, his body does not move without purpose,
bì yǐ cóng shī; but is certain to follow a teacher;
yán bù gǒu chū, his words do not come out carelessly,
bì yǐ bó wén; but are certain to come from extensive knowledge;
shìyǐ qíngxìng hé rén, thus, his emotions and nature are in harmony with people,
ér déyīn xiāng jì yě. and his virtuous reputation is passed down.
Confucius said:
"If you do not learn,
how can you act?
If you do not think,
how can you gain understanding?
Young men, strive for this,
and then you can be called teachers of men."
A horse, though it has swift feet,
but is not trained to the yoke,
then it will not become a good steed;
a person, though they have fine qualities,
but does not practice the Way,
then they will not become a *junzi* (gentleman);
therefore, the student seeks to practice the Way.
It is like the application of painted colors,
once the black and yellow colors are applied,
then the pure white essence is lost.
If something is ruined and does not change,
who will know its original nature?
Zǐxià said:
"Daily practice,
then learning will not be forgotten;
self-exhortation,
then the body will not fall into decline;
frequently hearing the great words of the world,
then one's ambition will become broader."
Therefore, the *junzi* in their learning,
their lack of懈怠 (xièdài, laxity),
It is like the movement of the heavens,
like the course of the sun and moon,
diligent throughout life,
stopping only after death;
therefore, even if one has the talent,
but lacks the will,
one cannot achieve one's accomplishments.
Willpower is the teacher of learning,
talent is the disciple of learning;
learners should not worry about a lack of talent,
but rather worry about a lack of resolve.
Therefore, there are countless people who try,
but few who succeed.
Therefore, the *jūnzǐ* must establish their will.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) says:
"The *jūnzǐ* strengthens himself tirelessly."
The completion of great music,
does not come from a single note;
the harmony of fine cuisine,
does not come from a single flavor;
the virtue of the sages,
does not come from a single principle.
Therefore, it is said:
learning is the means of encompassing all principles.
All principles are governed by one's heart,
all words are unified by one's mouth.
It depends on how one uses them,
In going forth, it brings great success;
in dwelling still, it benefits constancy;
in silence, images are established;
in speech, writings are formed.
Recounting the events of thousands of years ago,
it is as if they occurred at the same time;
discussing the customs of different places,
it is as if we are in the same room;
fathoming the reasons for the hidden and the manifest,
it is as if we see their true nature;
tracing the origins of order and chaos,
it is as if we are pointing at effects that are already apparent.
Therefore, the *Book of Poetry* says:
"Learning has a continuous brightness, like brilliant light."
This is what it means.
Now, solitary thought becomes stagnant and doesn't flow;
solitary action becomes difficult and doesn't succeed;
the human heart must have understanding,
and must have enlightenment.
It is like a fire that blazes fiercely when it gets wind,
like water rushing downwards and flowing swiftly.
Therefore, Tài Hào observed heaven and earth and drew the eight trigrams;
Suì Rén observed the seasons and drilled for fire;
Dì Xuān heard the phoenix cry and tuned the musical notes;
Cāng Jié observed the tracks of birds and created writing.
This is how the great sages learned from the divine and developed from the categories of things.
The wise cannot learn from afar,
Thus, one learns from what is near,
therefore, one takes sages as teachers.
In the past, Yán Yuān studied from sages;
upon hearing one thing, he understood ten.
Zǐ Gòng, upon hearing one thing, understood two.
Both of these men expanded their knowledge by analogy
and heard through earnest contemplation.
It is not only the worthy who learn from sages;
sages also learn from each other in succession.
Kǒngzǐ followed Wén and Wǔ,
Wén and Wǔ followed Chéng and Tāng,
Chéng and Tāng followed Xià Hòu,
Xià Hòu followed Yáo and Shùn.
Therefore, the Six Classics are books of mutual succession among the sages.
Although these men are gone,
their Way still exists.
If today's scholars diligently apply their minds to acquiring it,
they will certainly be able to attain brilliance and achieve broad understanding.
In all learning, the great principles come first,
and the names of things come after.
When the great principles are grasped, the names of things will follow.
However, the broad learning of vulgar scholars
is focused on the names of things,
detailed in instruments and mechanisms,
boastful in glosses and explanations,
picking out phrases and sentences,
but unable to grasp the ultimate point of the great principles to obtain the mind of the former kings.
This is no different from a female historian reciting the *Book of Odes* or a eunuch conveying commands.
Therefore, those who are made to study toil in thought but do not understand the Way;
they waste days and months without achieving success.
Thus, the gentleman must choose a teacher.
*Fǎ Xiàng Dì Èr* (Section on Exemplary Models, Part Two)
Establishing exemplary models is how one becomes a gentleman.
Of exemplary models, nothing is more important than rectifying one's appearance and being careful with one's deportment.
Therefore, when the former kings established ritual,
they created ceremonial caps and robes with emblems to distinguish them,
and pendant jade and sounding *huáng* ornaments to give them a sound,
desiring that they be respected,
desiring that they be solemn.
How can one be lax and negligent?
Appearance is the outward sign of a person.
When the outward sign is correct,
then one's emotions and nature are well-ordered.
When one's emotions and nature are well-ordered,
then benevolence and righteousness are preserved.
When benevolence and righteousness are preserved,
then eminent virtue is manifested.
When eminent virtue is manifested,
then one can become an exemplary model.
This is what is called a gentleman.
The gentleman possesses no land to be granted,
yet the myriad people respect him.
He has no intimidating power of punishment,
yet the myriad people fear him.
He has no music of pipes and flutes,
And the myriad people rejoice in him;
Without the reward of titles and emoluments,
The myriad people cherish him;
The reason for achieving this is the same.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"The gentleman is awe-inspiring but not fierce,
Composed but not arrogant."
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Revere your dignified demeanor,
That it may be a model for the people."
Now, if one neglects one's dignified demeanor,
Is careless in one's looking,
Is negligent in one's speech and commands,
And expects the people to take him as a model,
Such a thing has never happened.
If no one takes him as a model,
Then those who are disrespectful will arrive.
If the petty people are all disrespectful,
Then resentment toward others will be caused!
To lament one's own lowliness and not know the reason why,
Alas!
Therefore, the *Book of Documents* says:
"Only the sage, by forgetting contemplation, becomes mad;
Only the madman, by overcoming contemplation, becomes a sage."
That which human nature neglects
Exists in the subtle and hidden;
That which human emotions overlook
Exists in solitude.
Now, the hidden and subtle is the source of the manifest;
the solitary and isolated is the beginning of visibility.
How can it be simplified?
How can it be neglected?
Therefore, the superior man reveres solitude and is cautious of the hidden and subtle.
Even when in concealment,
spirits and gods cannot find a chink in his armor.
The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"Solemnly set is the rabbit net,
spread in the midst of the forest."
This speaks of being alone.
Moreover, there are those who cannot be disordered even in adversity,
these are Chéng Wáng and Jì Lù.
In the past, Chéng Wáng was about to die,
his body was arrayed in the ceremonial cap and robes,
only then did he issue the words of the "Gù Mìng" (Charge to the Heir).
Jì Lù encountered turmoil,
secured his cap strings before dying in the calamity of the naked blade.
In the adversity of impending death and the calamity of the naked blade,
they still did not forget reverence,
how much more so in relaxed feasting!
Therefore, the *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
"If it is deep,
use boats to cross it;
if it is shallow,
wade and swim across it."
This means one must certainly get across.
The gentleman's mouth utters no jesting words;
his words must have guard.
His person has no playful conduct;
his conduct must have restraint.
Words must have guard,
conduct must have restraint,
therefore even his wives and concubines cannot be taken liberties with,
even his friends cannot be treated with undue familiarity.
Thus, without anger or resentment, his virtuous conduct is practiced within the women's quarters;
without admonishment or instruction, his virtuous influence transforms the countryside.
The *Commentary* says, "The great man rectifies himself, and things of themselves become correct,"
this is what it means.
If even the commoner's residence is like this,
how much more so one who, being successful, practices (governance) in the world!
Therefore, Emperor Táng Yáo was truly respectful and yielding, and his brilliance covered the four directions;
Chéng Tāng dared not be negligent and thereby possessed all nine regions;
Wén Wáng was reverent and awe-struck and thus created that Xia territory.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"《Guān》 offers the libation but not the full sacrifice.
He is sincere, inspiring awe."
It speaks of transforming through observation from above.
The causes of calamity and failure
often have contemptuous disregard as the starting point;
how can one not be careful!
In the past, Sòng Mǐn had his head smashed in a board game,
Chén Líng suffered disaster because of jesting words,
Yán Bǐng created rebellion from mutual insult,
Zǐ Gōng was murdered by his son because of tasting turtle.
Therefore, when a gentleman conducts himself, he is humble;
when facing an enemy, he yields;
when dealing with subordinates, he is dignified;
when serving superiors, he is respectful.
When these four are complete, resentment and blame do not arise,
and blessings and emoluments follow.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Be respectfully diligent in your position,
and be upright in what you support.
The spirits will listen to you,
and thereby grant you goodness."
Therefore, when a gentleman interacts with people,
he is joyful but not overly familiar,
harmonious but not uniform;
he is friendly but not flattering or deceitful,
he learns but does not act superficially;
he is easy to approach but difficult to flatter,
he has many grievances but few faults;
therefore, he does not sever friendships,
nor does he betray his friends.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Be careful at the beginning and reverent at the end,
so as not to be in difficulty."
Now, ritual is something
that people urgently need;
it can be practiced throughout one's life,
and cannot be separated from even for a moment.
If one separates from it for a moment,
Zé tāomàn zhī xíng zhēn yān; [Then arrogant and disrespectful behavior will arrive.]
xūyú wàng, [If (one) forgets even for a moment,]
zé tāomàn zhī xīn shēng yān; [then arrogant and disrespectful thoughts will arise.]
kuàng wúlǐ ér kěyǐ zhōngshǐ hū! [How much less can one complete anything from beginning to end without propriety!]
Fú lǐ yě zhě, jìng zhī jīng yě, [Now, propriety is the framework of respect,]
jìng yě zhě, lǐ zhī qíng yě. [and respect is the essence of propriety.]
Wújìng wú yǐ xíng lǐ, [Without respect, there is no way to practice propriety,]
wúlǐ wú yǐ jié jìng; [without propriety, there is no way to regulate respect.]
Dào bù piānfèi, [The Way should not be partially abandoned,]
xiāng xū ér xíng. [but proceed in mutual dependence.]
Shìgù néng jìn jìng yǐ cóng lǐ zhě, [Therefore, those who can exhaust their respect to follow propriety,]
wèi zhī chéngrén; [are called accomplished persons.]
guò zé shēng luàn, [If one goes too far, then disorder arises,]
luàn zé zāi jí qí shēn. [and disorder will bring calamity to one's person.]
Xī Jìn Hùigōng yǐ màn duān ér wúsì, [In the past, Duke Hùi of Jìn initiated arrogance and had no heir,]
Wén Gōng yǐ sù mìng ér xīng guó; [Duke Wén rose to power because he handled orders with solemnity;]
Xì Chōu yǐ ào xiǎng zhēng wáng, [Xì Chōu invited ruin by enjoying his prosperity with arrogance,]
Jì Quē yǐ jìng qī shòu fú; [Jì Quē received investiture because he respected his wife.]
Zǐ Wéi yǐ "Dàmíng" zhāo luàn, [Zǐ Wéi incited disorder with the "Dàmíng" ode,]
Wěi Bà yǐ "Jì Zuì" bǎo lù, [Wěi Bà preserved his emolument with the "Jì Zuì" ode,]
Liáng Xiāo yǐ "Chún Bēn" sàng jiā, [Liáng Xiāo lost his family with the "Chún Bēn" ode,]
Zǐ Zhǎn yǐ "Cǎochóng" chāng zú. [Zǐ Zhǎn brought prosperity to his clan with the "Cǎochóng" ode.]
Jūnzǐ gǎn xiōng dé zhī rú bǐ, [The noble man is moved by the fact that evil virtues are like that,]
jiàn jí dé zhī rúcǐ. [and sees that good virtues are like this.]
Gù lì bì qìngzhé, [Therefore, when standing, one must be bent over,]
zuò bì bào gǔ; [when sitting, one must embrace the drum.]
zhōuxuán zhōng guī, [Turning around must accord with the compass,]
His turning and maneuvering are in accordance with the square;
his gaze does not stray from the area defined by the knotting of the girdle and the embroidery of the robe;
his words do not exceed the rank indicated by his insignia.
His voice and breath are exemplary,
his spirit is lovable,
his bowing and raising of the head are worthy of emulation,
Gù yú Lǔ yě,
minor evils were surely recorded;
regarding the various states,
major evils were first written down.
To see others but not see oneself is called blindness;
to hear others but not hear oneself is called deafness;
to consider others but not consider oneself is called confusion.
Therefore, there is no greater clarity than seeing oneself,
no greater acuteness of hearing than hearing oneself,
no greater sagacity than considering oneself.
These three things, lifting them up is very light,
doing them is very near,
yet people do not know them.
Therefore, the wise lift up very light things to undertake the heaviness of the world,
travel very near roads to exhaust the distances of the world.
Therefore, the more elevated the virtue, the more solid the foundation;
the more numerous the victories, the more expansive the love.
The *Book of Changes* says:
“*Return (Fù)* brings success.
Going out and coming in without error.
Friends come without blame.”
Is this not what it means!
A junzi (gentleman) regarding himself
is without anything that he does not fear.
If I have good qualities,
I fear that others will not admire me;
if I have bad qualities,
I fear that others will not dislike me.
Seeing the good in others,
I fear that I will not be able to cultivate it;
seeing the bad in others,
I fear that I will surely be like them.
Therefore, his inclination towards the Dao,
his yielding and deferring are admirable,
his narratives and writings are methodical,
his movement and stillness are consistent,
his leading in rites is not neglectful,
therefore, he is the hope of the masses.
"Cultivating the Root, Section 3"
People’s hearts invariably possess reason and principle,
but when it comes to employing them, they differ.
Some employ them for themselves,
some employ them for others;
employing them for oneself is called attending to the root,
employing them for others is called approaching the branches.
When a gentleman governs,
he first attends to the root,
therefore virtue is established and resentment is lessened.
When a petty person governs,
he first approaches the branches,
therefore accomplishments are abandoned and enmity increases.
In Kǒngzǐ's compiling of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
he details what is internal and omits what is external,
he is strict with himself and lenient with others,
